newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon votes for new parliament on Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon votes for new parliament on Saturday.

text.p: Cameroon votes for a new parliament on Saturday with President Paul Biya's party counting on opposition divisions to bring it victory.
Biya's Cameroon People's Democratic Rally (RDPC) says it is aiming for an absolute majority of 91 of the new national assembly's 180 seats.
But the opposition Social Democratic Front (SDF), which has its power base in the volatile English-speaking North-West Province, says it will get more seats than the RDPC.
"We will obtain at least 100 seats," Front leader and opposition stalwart John Fru Ndi told Reuters.

The Front boycotted the 1992 general election but Fru Ndi received 35 percent of votes in the presidential election that Biya won in the same year. The opposition, not for the first time, cried fraud.
North-West province, under overnight curfew after attacks by suspected separatists on security forces in March, is a flashpoint in the largely French-speaking Central African country.

The Front is not only popular in its stronghold there but also among Cameroon's main ethnic Bamileke group and the urban poor. It polled well during January municipal elections, taking the nation's biggest city, the port of Douala.
The ruling party was equally confident of victory.

"We are targeting an absolute majority of at least 91 seats. Our popularity has improved. In the north, south and east we will obtain two-thirds of the seats," Azu'u Fonkam, coordinator of the party's election commission, told Reuters.
"The advantage is that, where we will be losing, the opposition will divide the seats," he added.
Biya, who took over from independence president Ahmadou Ahidjo in 1982, faces a presidential election in October.
In the 1992 election, his party won 88 seats. It formed an alliance with the small Movement for the Defence of the Republic (MDR) to ensure a majority.
Polls open at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) on Saturday and close at 6 p.m. (1700 GMT). A total of 45 parties will field 1,800 candidates to contest the seats.
All travel by road, rail or air between Cameroon's cities is prohibited to stop parties busing in voters.
Election officials say first results may trickle out on Saturday but it may be days before a clear picture emerges.
International observers described the 1992 poll as "seriously flawed" and "very problematic".

London-based Amnesty International, highlighting fresh human rights violations in Cameroon, urged Biya's government to ensure that all citizens could vote without fear of arrest, detention or ill-treatment.
The main problem this time appeared to be distribution of voter cards -- a common problem in African elections. Opposition leaders say their supporters have had particular problems.
The precise number of voters remains unclear. About four million people were eligible to vote in the municipal polls.
Election officials predict about 3.9 million voters will have registered for the parliamentary poll.

"The lists from the South-West province have not yet arrived, which is very unfortunate. There are many isolated areas there," said Erik Essousse, deputy director for elections at the Ministry of Territorial Administration (Interior).
